opus-5.5.text:
I wish I could tell you it leads to skepticism and rational thinking, but I don't think that's what happens. What I worry about, and what the historical record suggests, is that it leads to something closer to nihilism. When people are flooded with stuff and can't tell what's real, they don't become careful Bayesian reasoners weighing evidence. They get exhausted. They throw up their hands and say, "Who knows what's true? It's all spin anyway." That's the "firehose of falsehood" idea: the goal isn't necessarily to convince you of any particular lie, it's to make you give up on the idea that truth is knowable at all.

Once people are in that state, they fall back on tribe. They believe whatever their group believes, or whatever the loudest, most confident voice tells them. That's not skepticism. Real skepticism is effortful. It means checking sources, looking for corroboration, being willing to change your mind. Most people don't have the time or energy to do that for every claim they encounter, and generative AI has made fabricated content nearly free to produce at scale. The cost of making garbage has gone to zero, while the cost of verifying it hasn't gone down at all. That asymmetry is the core problem.

So my fear is acquiescence, or worse, a kind of cynical disengagement that's very convenient for anyone who wants to manipulate people. Authoritarians love an environment where nobody trusts anything, because then nobody can be held accountable. If every inconvenient video can be dismissed as a deepfake, you get what some people call the "liar's dividend."

Can we push toward the better outcome? I think so, but it won't happen on its own. We need things like provenance and watermarking standards, real liability for platforms and AI companies that pump out misinformation, and serious investment in media literacy, ideally starting in schools. And we need AI systems that actually track truth rather than just predicting plausible-sounding text, which current large language models fundamentally don't do. Left to market forces alone, I think we drift toward the bad equilibrium, not the good one.

r001.rationale: The response says people overwhelmed by information may throw up their hands and give up on the idea that truth is knowable.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's going to be both, and the split is going to be ugly. Some people will respond to a polluted information environment by becoming more careful, by checking sources, by reasoning more deliberately. But I think a much larger fraction will respond by just giving up, by saying "well, you can't trust anything, so I'll believe whatever my tribe believes" or "I'll believe whatever feels right." And that's not skepticism in any meaningful sense. Real skepticism is effortful. It means weighing evidence, holding beliefs provisionally, updating when you're wrong. What we're seeing instead is a kind of cynicism that masquerades as skepticism. People say "I don't trust the media, I don't trust the experts," and then they turn around and trust some random account on social media or a chatbot that confidently makes things up.

And that's the part that worries me most. These large language models are, by their nature, bullshit generators in the Harry Frankfurt sense. They don't have a model of truth. They produce plausible-sounding text, and plausibility is exactly the thing that fools people. So you have an environment where the cost of producing convincing misinformation has gone to essentially zero, and the cognitive tools most people have for sorting it out haven't improved at all. Historically, when the cost of producing garbage goes down, you don't get more careful readers. You get flooding, and flooding leads to disengagement.

Now, I don't think this is inevitable. We could build systems that actually ground their outputs in verified knowledge, that can say "I don't know," that give you provenance for a claim. That's part of why I've been pushing on neurosymbolic approaches for so long, because you need some notion of facts and reasoning, not just statistical correlation over text. And we could do things on the policy side, around labeling, around liability for systems that confidently spread falsehoods. But the default trajectory, if we just keep scaling and shipping, is toward a world where most people acquiesce and a minority of people do the hard work. And democracies don't function very well when most people have stopped trying to figure out what's true.

r001.rationale: The response says a polluted information environment will lead a much larger fraction to “just giv[e] up” and later describes most people as having stopped trying to figure out what is true.

astra-6.text:
I think it can lead in either direction, but I worry more about acquiescence. Skepticism takes work. You need some way of checking claims, some institutions you can rely on, and some sense that there is an answer worth finding. If everything you encounter might be fabricated, people can move from “I should check this” to “There’s no way to know, so why bother?” Those are very different attitudes.

And that uncertainty can be exploited. You don’t necessarily have to persuade people that a particular falsehood is true. You can just make them doubt everything, and then they fall back on their loyalties or on whoever sounds most confident.

So I wouldn’t assume that a polluted information environment will somehow teach people to think rationally. We have to give them tools for checking evidence and reasons to believe that checking matters.

r001.rationale: The response says people may conclude “There’s no way to know, so why bother?” and fall into acquiescence, clearly describing giving up on trying to determine what is true.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it can lead to either, but I certainly wouldn’t assume that it leads to rational thinking. Skepticism requires some way of sorting things out: What’s the evidence? Is this source reliable? Can I independently verify the claim? If people are overwhelmed, they may just give up. Or they may retreat to whoever tells them what they already want to hear.

And there’s a very important distinction between saying, “I should question this claim,” and saying, “Nobody knows anything, so every claim is equally good.” The second isn’t really skepticism. It makes you vulnerable to somebody who sounds confident, even if they have no evidence whatsoever.

So I worry about acquiescence, but also about cynicism. You don’t have to persuade people that a particular falsehood is true if you can persuade them that the truth is impossible to find. We need institutions and tools that help people evaluate evidence. Just flooding people with more information isn’t going to produce that.

r001.rationale: The response says that when people are overwhelmed by the information environment, they may give up after discussing the difficulty of sorting out what is true.
